pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — round decimals to any place using place-value understanding; round any whole number to a required degree of accuracy.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y6 'round any whole number to a required degree of accuracy'; Y5 round decimals with two places to the nearest whole number and to one decimal place.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.A.4 'Use place value understanding to round decimals to any place' and 4.NBT.A.3 round multi-digit whole numbers to any place.
• Operational details: Round via NEARNESS on a number line — locate the number between the two candidate rounding points, find the midpoint, and decide which it is nearer. Derive the 'look at the next digit' rule FROM the midpoint (5-and-above is at/past halfway) rather than teaching it as an unexplained rule. Cover rounding both decimals (to dp) and large whole numbers (to nearest 10^k), and rounding for estimation (4.83×2.17 ≈ 5×2).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'Round 3.46 to 1 dp.' Tier B: 'Round 7,654,321 to the nearest 100,000 and justify with the midpoint.' Tier C: 'Round 3.4567 to 2 dp and explain which digit decides it.'
bestPractices: Round as a nearness decision on a number line: mark the two candidate values, mark the midpoint, place the number, decide which it is closer to
Derive the next-digit rule from the midpoint (≥5 means at or past halfway → round up), rather than asserting it
Practise rounding decimals to a stated dp AND whole numbers to a stated place with the same nearness logic
Address the boundary/round-up cascade explicitly (rounding 3.798 to 2 dp → 3.80, and 9.96 → 10.0)
Connect rounding to estimation — round each factor to check a calculation — so rounding has a purpose beyond the drill
keyRepresentations: Number line with the two rounding candidates and a marked midpoint
Place-value chart to isolate the rounding place and the deciding next digit
'Rounding hill/valley' visual (nearer candidate is downhill) for the midpoint decision
Estimation strips pairing rounded factors with the exact calculation
commonMisconceptions: Rounding digit-by-digit / double rounding (3.4567 → 3.457 → 3.46 → 3.5) instead of one decision at the target place
'Always round 5 down' or inconsistent treatment of the exact-midpoint case
Truncating (chopping) rather than rounding (3.48 → 3.4 to 1 dp)
Forgetting the round-up cascade across a 9 (3.798 to 2 dp → 3.80, not 3.79 or 3.710)
Dropping the trailing zero that records the rounded place (writing 3.8 for 3.80 to 2 dp when the place must be shown)

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: round decimals to any place and whole numbers to a required degree of accuracy by treating rounding as a nearness decision on a number line. Learners locate the number between its two candidate rounding points, find the midpoint, and decide which it is nearer — deriving the 'look at the next digit' rule from the midpoint rather than memorising it. Work covers decimals to a stated number of places, large whole numbers to a stated place, carry/round-up cascades over a 9, placeholder zeros, the risk of double rounding, and rounding for estimation.

activities.title: Rounding as a nearness decision on a number line
feedback: If the learner chops instead of rounding (e.g. 3.4567 to 2 dp written as 3.45), have them look at the digit just past the cut: 6 ≥ 5 means 3.4567 is past the midpoint 3.455 and so is nearer 3.46. Place it between 3.45 and 3.46 to see which is closer. (To 1 dp, chopping would give 3.4, but the correct answer is 3.5.)

If they round digit-by-digit (double rounding), use 3.4547 to 2 dp to show why it fails: rounding to 3 dp first gives 3.455, which then rounds up to 3.46, but a single decision at the hundredths place (decider thousandths 4 < 5) gives 3.45. Double rounding changed the answer — compare the full number to the single midpoint for the target place.
When a carry crosses a 9 (3.798 → 3.80), confirm the trailing zero stays because '2 decimal places' means two digits after the point.
If they are unsure about the exact-midpoint case, reinforce that at the midpoint and beyond the number rounds up to the higher candidate.
activities.rationale: Deriving the next-digit rule from the midpoint gives the procedure a reason, directly targeting double-rounding and 'always round 5 down' errors; the 3.4547 contrast makes the double-rounding hazard observable because the two routes disagree. An interactive number line that auto-brackets candidates, marks the midpoint, lets the learner place the number, lights the nearer segment, and highlights the deciding digit can make the nearness judgement concrete; these interaction examples are optional ways to realise the mechanism, not requirements.
learnerActions: Pick a target precision (e.g. 1 decimal place) and draw a number line showing the two candidate values the number sits between — for 3.4567 to 1 dp, that is 3.4 and 3.5.
Mark the midpoint of the segment (3.45) clearly.
Place the number on the line (3.4567 lands just past the midpoint) and state which candidate it is nearer to.
State the rounded result (3.5) and point to the digit that decided it (the hundredths digit, 5, sits at/past halfway).
Repeat in whole-number mode: bracket 7,654,321 between 7,600,000 and 7,700,000, mark the midpoint 7,650,000, place the number, and round to the nearest 100,000 (7,700,000).
Try a round-up cascade: place 3.798 to round to 2 dp between 3.79 and 3.80, see it is nearer 3.80, and write the trailing zero.

Compare two routes for rounding 3.4547 to 2 dp: round straight to 2 dp (decider is the thousandths 4, so 3.45) and also round to 3 dp first (3.455) then to 2 dp (3.46). Notice the answers differ — so make one decision at the target place, not a chain of roundings.
activities.intendedInsight: The midpoint IS the '5-and-above' rule: a number at or past halfway rounds up to the higher candidate. Rounding is one decision made at the target place by comparing nearness, not a digit-by-digit chop — and chopping or double rounding can give a different, wrong answer.

activities.title: Isolating the deciding digit with a place-value chart
feedback: If the learner gives 3.5 when 2 dp is asked, have them count decimal digits: 2 dp needs two, so the answer is 3.46.
If the wrong place is read for a large number, re-anchor on the chart: find the hundred-thousands column, then look one column to its right (the ten-thousands digit decides).
Keep the focus on the single decider digit, not on re-rounding digits further along.
activities.rationale: A place-value chart separates the target place from its decider, addressing wrong-precision errors and misreading places in large numbers. A static chart illustrates a case clearly; it is a scaffold that does not by itself let learners test arbitrary numbers or feel the boundary cascade.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.4: use place value understanding to round decimals to any place; 4.NBT.A.3 round multi-digit whole numbers to any place.
learnerActions: Write the number in a place-value chart spanning the decimal point.
Circle the place you must round to and underline the single digit immediately beyond it — the decider.
Round 3.4567 to 2 dp (3.46) and say which digit decided it (the 6 in the thousandths).
Round 7,654,321 to the nearest 100,000 (7,700,000) and name the deciding digit (the ten-thousands digit, 5).
Count the digits after the point aloud to confirm you gave the asked-for precision (e.g. 2 dp means exactly two decimal digits).
activities.intendedInsight: Only the digit one place beyond the required accuracy decides the rounding; naming the target place prevents rounding to the wrong precision.

activities.title: Keeping placeholder zeros after a carry
feedback: If the learner writes 2.4 for 2.397 to 2 dp, point out it now shows only one decimal place; the correct answer is 2.40.
Distinguish this from a rounding mistake — the rounding was right, only the recorded precision is missing the zero.
For 9.96 → 10.0, confirm the whole-number carry still leaves a tenths place that must read 0.
activities.rationale: Carries that produce placeholder zeros are a distinct performance slip from the rounding decision itself, so they need their own targeted practice.
learnerActions: Round 2.397 to 2 dp. The hundredths carry gives 2.40 — write the final 0.
Explain why 2.4 would be wrong for '2 decimal places' even though the value looks the same.
Round 9.96 to 1 dp (10.0) and keep the tenths zero.
Check each answer by counting that it shows exactly the required number of decimal places.
activities.intendedInsight: A rounded answer must display the required place even when a carry produces a zero there; the trailing zero records the precision, so dropping it changes what the answer claims.

activities.title: Rounding to estimate a calculation
feedback: If the estimate is far from the exact answer, check whether each factor was rounded to a sensible place.
Encourage stating the chosen rounding place so the estimate's accuracy can be judged.
activities.rationale: Connecting rounding to estimation gives the skill a real use and reinforces the nearness idea across operations.
learnerActions: Round each factor of 4.83 × 2.17 to a convenient value (5 × 2) and compute the estimate (10).
Compare your estimate to the exact product once calculated (≈ 10.48) and say whether the estimate is reasonable.
Try estimating another product or sum by rounding each number first, and state which place you rounded to and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding has a purpose beyond drill: it gives quick, sensible estimates to check whether an exact calculation is plausible.

constraints: Multiple-choice, slider, and fill-in response formats can consolidate and check rounding outcomes (e.g. a truncation distractor of 3.4 for 3.48), but recognising a correct rounded value does not by itself show the learner is reasoning from the midpoint; pair outcome checks with working that reveals the method.
A static annotated number line illustrates a single rounding case but does not let the learner test arbitrary numbers or experience a boundary cascade; use it as a scaffold, not the whole lesson.

Dialogue prompts (e.g. 'you rounded 3.4567 to 3.46 — walk me through why, not digit by digit') can surface double-rounding and truncation errors; the nearness decision can also be made where the number is placed and compared spatially.
Round in one decision at the target place; do not round digit-by-digit (double rounding) and do not truncate.
Treat the exact midpoint and above as rounding up to the higher candidate; avoid 'always round 5 down'.
Preserve trailing/placeholder zeros that record the required place (2.40, not 2.4; 10.0, not 10).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source marks the Common Core claim as verified:false and the DfE claim as verified:true; confidence of the original row was 'high'. No new verification has been performed here.

Self-audit: 3.4567 to 2 dp = 3.46 (decider 6 ≥ 5); to 1 dp = 3.5 (candidates 3.4/3.5, midpoint 3.45). 3.4547 to 2 dp = 3.45 directly, but 3.455 then 3.46 by double rounding (illustrates the hazard). 2.397 to 2 dp = 2.40 (carry keeps placeholder zero). 7,654,321 to nearest 100,000: midpoint 7,650,000, value above it, rounds to 7,700,000 (decider ten-thousands digit 5). 3.798 to 2 dp = 3.80. 9.96 to 1 dp = 10.0. 4.83×2.17 ≈ 5×2 = 10 (exact ≈ 10.48). All consistent and checked.

The original row and recommendation wrote the 1-dp candidates as '3.40 and 3.50', displaying two decimal places for a one-decimal-place rounding; corrected in the learner action to '3.4 and 3.5' (midpoint 3.45) to avoid reinforcing a precision confusion.

Activity 1's sourceClaims were set to [] because its rationale is a number-line/midpoint-derivation teaching principle that neither curriculum claim directly supports (the claims establish the topic/standard, not that pedagogy). The place-value-chart activity retains the CCSS 'use place value understanding' claim, which does support its principle.
The original diagnostic listed '2.40 (keeping the final zero)' for rounding 2.397 to 2 dp, which is correct; retained as the placeholder-zero teaching point.
The non-preferred 3D option was dropped because the source itself only noted it adds nothing for a one-dimensional number-line task; no universal claim about 3D is asserted.

probeDeeper: Round 2.397 to 2 dp — why must you keep the 0 on the end?
Round 3.4547 to 3 dp first, then to 2 dp. Now round 3.4547 straight to 2 dp — same answer? (double-rounding)
Round 7,654,321 to the nearest 100,000 — which digit decides?
assess.correctAnswer: 3.46; 2.40 (keeping the final zero); 7,700,000 — deciding by the digit one place beyond the required accuracy.

errorPatterns.pattern: Truncates instead of rounding: chops 3.4567 to 3.45 rather than 3.46
errorPatterns.nextMove: Look at the digit just past the cut (6 ≥ 5 → round up). Place 3.4567 between 3.45 and 3.46 on a number line to see which is nearer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The kept digits are correct but never rounded up when the next digit is 5 or more.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the placeholder zero after a carry: writes 2.4 for 2.397 to 2 dp, so it no longer shows 2 decimal places
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach rounding — note that '2 dp' means two digits after the point, so the carried result is 2.40; the 0 must stay.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer to 2 dp has only one decimal digit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds to the wrong precision — gives 1 dp when 2 dp is asked, or reads the wrong place for large numbers
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the required place, then its decider digit; count decimal places explicitly. Reground with a place-value chart spanning the decimal point.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 3.4567 comes back as 3.5, or the whole number is rounded to the wrong place.

responseLevels.gap: Truncates instead of rounding, or rounds to the wrong precision.
responseLevels.full: Rounds decimals to any number of places and whole numbers to any place, handling carries and placeholder zeros, and avoids double-rounding.
responseLevels.partial: Rounds simple cases but drops carried placeholder zeros or slips on the required number of places.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the task and watch the working: 'Round 3.4567 to 2 decimal places. Round 2.397 to 2 decimal places. Round 7,654,321 to the nearest 100,000.' Watch whether they round or chop, and what they do at the carry.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 3.4567 distinguishes rounding from truncating (3.46 vs 3.45); 2.397 forces a carry that produces a placeholder zero the child must keep to show 2 dp (2.40, not 2.4); the whole-number item checks the same rule transfers to large places. Watching reveals which mechanism is running.
